articles.title: Ohio State men's basketball coach Jake Diebler faces talent overload challenge this season
articles.summary: Diebler is dealing with the issue of having too much talent on his roster, which he believes is a good problem to have.
articles.content: Ohio State men's basketball coach Jake Diebler is dealing with a new challenge this season: having too much talent on his roster. The Buckeyes' depth has been a welcome change from last year, when they struggled to find contributors off the bench, ultimately impacting their performance in the 2026 NCAA Tournament. To address this issue, Diebler and his staff brought in nine new players, many of whom are expected to make significant contributions this season. However, during a recent game against Prairie View A&M on November 16th, Diebler was reminded that having too many options can be just as problematic as not enough. Eleven different Buckeyes saw action for at least three and a quarter minutes in the first half of the game, which Ohio State narrowly won 34-29. The coach made adjustments by shortening his rotation in the second half, allowing the team to pull ahead comfortably with an 86-59 win over Prairie View A&M. Diebler pointed out that many players saw action in the first half and noted that the coaches were still figuring out their rotations. Ohio State's coaching staff is still figuring out their rotations after the first few games of the season. With a mix of experienced players and newcomers, it's not surprising that Diebler is facing a daunting task in trimming his rotation down to a manageable size. As he noted, having too many options can be both a blessing and a curse - but ultimately, he believes it's a good problem to have. Diebler is getting ready for the team's next high-major showdown against Vanderbilt on November 24th, after which point he'll likely have to make some tough decisions about who gets playing time. The second half of the Prairie View A&M game provided a glimpse into how Diebler plans to approach this challenge - with three players not seeing action until the lead was at least 19 points ahead and halfway through the second half. Diebler is also using practices as an opportunity to experiment with different lineups and minute allocations, in addition to monitoring player performance on game days. Ohio State still has a few more games against mid-major teams before facing top-tier opponents again, which should give Diebler some extra time to fine-tune his rotation decisions. The arrival of Lee Aaliya has presented a challenge for Ohio State's coaching staff as they navigate the optimal roster size. Aaliya, an experienced international forward, had been making progress in preseason before his playing time was limited due to illness. His relatively short playing time so far, just 17:15 minutes across four appearances, suggests he may not be ready to contribute at a high level yet. The coaching staff is optimistic about Aaliya's potential, but they acknowledge the need for him to make more of an impact in practice before being given more game time. Diebler emphasized that assessing Aaliya's contributions should focus on his performance during practices rather than his limited minutes so far. He suggested that this approach would allow them to gauge his readiness and progress without rushing him back into action. The head coach also pointed out that the roster is currently overburdened, with multiple players sharing playing time in each game. This has resulted in a situation where at least 10 different players have scored points in three of Ohio State's first five games this season. Ohio State's coaching staff will soon face a crucial decision regarding their playing rotation. The team has seen an unusually high number of players scoring points in recent games, and coach Diebler believes that this trend must be addressed promptly to avoid hindering the team's growth. Diebler emphasized that every game is now crucial for Ohio State, and any delay in making tough decisions could have long-term consequences for the team's development. articles.title: Lunar Regolith Simulants Support Potato Growth with Organic Matter Addition
articles.summary: Researchers at Oregon State University have found that potatoes can grow well in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter.
articles.content: Researchers at Oregon State University have made significant progress towards establishing reliable food production systems for long-term human exploration of the moon. According to Aymeric Goyer, a member of the university's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter. This breakthrough is crucial as NASA aims to establish a sustained human presence on the moon through its Artemis program. One of the key challenges facing this goal is food production, instead of relying on expensive resupply missions from Earth, astronauts will need to be able to grow their own food. The lunar regolith, a layer of loose rock and dust that covers most of the moon's surface, poses significant obstacles for plant growth due to its very low levels of organic matter. To overcome this challenge, researchers have been experimenting with adding nutrient-rich organic soil amendments to simulated lunar soil. In a recent paper published in npj Microgravity, Goyer and his colleagues at Oregon State tested the effects of different levels of vermicompost, an organic amendment produced by breaking down organic matter using earthworms, on potato growth in lunar regolith simulants. In a bid to make space travel more sustainable, scientists have been exploring ways to create fertile soil for growing crops on the moon. One potential solution is to bring organic matter from Earth and convert it into more using food scraps and plant waste. The researchers tested five different types of regolith simulants, which mimic the varying conditions found across the lunar surface. They also included a sample of soil from Oregon's Hermiston region, known for its high potato yields on Earth. This allowed them to compare how potatoes grow in simulated lunar conditions with those grown in normal Earth soils. The addition of organic matter was found to have a significant impact on plant growth. In particular, the researchers discovered that adding 30% vermicompost to the regolith simulant resulted in plants that matched their Earth-grown counterparts in terms of size and root development. However, using less than 15% vermicompost had only partial benefits for plant growth, while growing without it altogether led to stunted roots and underdeveloped plants. The nutritional quality of potatoes grown in simulated lunar soil was found to be comparable to those cultivated on Earth. Notably, the amount of glycoalkaloids - naturally occurring toxins that can cause green discoloration beneath the skin - remained unchanged in potatoes grown in these conditions. Researchers chose potatoes for their experiments due to their high calorie yield per unit of land and substantial nutritional value, making them a practical choice for long-duration space missions. articles.title: Apple's HomeView Smart Display Difficult to Disassemble
articles.summary: iFixit's teardown analysis reveals Apple's latest smart display is held together with exceptionally strong adhesive making it difficult to repair without causing damage.
articles.content: Apple's latest smart display, HomeView, has been put to the test by iFixit, a company known for its detailed device teardowns. However, unlike previous Apple products, HomeView proved to be extremely difficult to disassemble without causing damage. The analysis revealed that HomeView is held together with an exceptionally strong adhesive. This development may seem alarming, but it's not necessarily cause for concern according to some experts. The reason being that many people who purchase Apple devices don't intend to perform repairs themselves and therefore won't be impacted by the difficulties of accessing components. The right to repair has become a significant issue in recent years, particularly with regards to electronic devices like smartphones and laptops. Advocates argue that users should have the ability to fix their own devices rather than relying on manufacturers or professional services. This not only empowers consumers but also creates a secondary market for repairs. Apple's stance on this issue is complex. On one hand, the company has made efforts in the past to make certain products more repair-friendly. For instance, the EU has mandated that Apple allow iPhone battery replacements by 2027. However, HomeView takes a step back from these advancements with its use of extremely strong adhesives. The consequences of this design choice are clear: when repairs become necessary, they will be time-consuming and challenging. iFixit's analysis warns that the process will not be "easy or pleasant" due to the tight bonding between components. The repair costs for a HomeView device that has fallen out of warranty can be substantial, potentially reaching as much as the device's original price tag of $299. This reality is unlikely to deter users who purchase smart displays like HomeView from considering their long-term maintenance needs. Unlike smartphones and laptops, which are often subject to rough handling and environmental stressors, smart displays tend to remain stationary in a single location. The absence of a replaceable battery, for instance, means that users won't need to worry about routine battery replacements or power-related issues. Furthermore, the custom 7-inch display on HomeView is not available as an aftermarket replacement option from third-party vendors. The reliability of smart display speakers is a well-known issue in the tech world. iFixit's report highlights that embedded speakers are prone to failure, and those inside the HomeView resemble laptop speakers rather than the high-quality tweeters found in Apple's HomePod. Testing various smart displays and speakers has shown that speaker failures are relatively rare, especially when handled with care. In fact, scouring online forums like the HomePod subreddit reveals few instances of blown or faulty speakers - and most of these cases involve users who have tampered with their devices by installing third-party components. Despite concerns over repair difficulties, a more pressing issue is the compact 7-inch screen on the HomeView, which feels cramped for video watching compared to larger displays like those found in Amazon's Echo Show lineup. articles.title: Neglecting Candidate Experience Can Undermine Employer Brand
articles.summary: Employers often neglect the candidate experience, focusing on branding without considering its impact on job applicants.
articles.content: Job seekers who invest hours in researching a company, preparing for interviews, and providing references often receive abrupt rejection emails or worse, complete radio silence. The indifference of not even acknowledging the effort put into the hiring process can be more hurtful than the rejection itself. Employers spend considerable resources building their employer brands to attract top talent, but neglecting the candidate experience can undermine these efforts. A lack of personal touch in rejection emails can make a company seem uncaring and impersonal, which may deter future job applicants. Career expert Vicki Salemi notes that employers often focus on branding without considering its impact on the candidate experience. By prioritizing one over the other, companies risk losing out on potential hires who are turned off by poor treatment during the hiring process. The consequences of neglecting the candidate experience can be significant for both future hires and customers. A generic rejection email can damage a company's reputation and make it less appealing to prospective employees. A study published in February found that personalized rejection messages can help preserve a company's attractiveness, while impersonal ones can have the opposite effect. This suggests that taking the time to craft a thoughtful message is crucial for maintaining a positive employer brand. When crafting a rejection email, employers often focus on getting it over with quickly rather than putting thought into its content. However, a strong employer brand is at stake in every interaction with potential employees, including those who don't make the cut for a particular role. In a study of 236 working adults and final-year students in the Netherlands and Belgium, researchers found that rejection emails can have a lasting impact on how job seekers perceive an employer. Participants presented with a company known for its strong employer brand saw their attractiveness scores drop significantly after receiving a standard rejection letter. The score fell from 3.29 to 2.61. A few days later, the score had partially recovered but still remained below its original level. This suggests that taking the time to craft a thoughtful message is crucial for maintaining a positive employer brand. In an appreciative rejection letter, however, participants showed no statistically significant decline in their perception of the employer, indicating that empathy can go a long way in preserving a strong reputation. The consequences of a poor candidate experience extend far beyond hiring. It can lead to lost business and damaged reputations. A negative hiring experience can have far-reaching consequences for businesses. Research suggests that nearly a third of job seekers who had a bad experience would stop buying from that company altogether. Those who feel dismissed by potential employers are likely to discourage others from applying as well. This word-of-mouth can spread quickly, potentially damaging the company's reputation and impacting its bottom line. The failure to send thoughtful rejection emails is often cited as a reason for this negative fallout. Despite being quick and easy to do, many employers still neglect to send these emails, leaving candidates feeling undervalued and unappreciated. Recruiters may claim that they are too busy managing multiple job openings to send personalized rejection messages. However, technology can actually make the task easier, allowing recruiters to draft and send emails with greater efficiency. AI-powered tools can even help recruiters tailor their rejection emails to each candidate's strengths and areas for development, ensuring that every communication is meaningful and respectful. The rejection process in job hiring is often seen as a necessary evil, but it can also be a missed opportunity to build relationships and maintain a positive reputation. Leadership plays a crucial role in setting the tone for how companies approach rejecting candidates, with company culture being a key factor in determining the level of accountability shown. This trickle-down effect means that if leadership is not invested in transparency and respect, rejection emails may suffer as a result. A particularly egregious example of a rejection email was shared by Salemi, which lacked basic details such as the candidate's name or position applied for, but still managed to provide some closure by giving an answer. This brief acknowledgment is a low bar for job seekers who have invested significant time in the hiring process. According to career expert Jasmine Escalera, even a simple rejection letter can be beneficial to candidates, providing them with closure and helping them focus their efforts on other opportunities. However, this basic level of communication is often lacking in automated messages sent to candidates after multiple rounds of interviews. A more thoughtful approach was demonstrated by Fijneman-Ghielen's study, which showed an appreciative rejection letter that acknowledged the candidate's interest and effort, explained the reason for not moving forward, and even offered a discount code as a gesture of appreciation. Employers can soften the blow of rejection by expressing appreciation for a candidate's skills and effort, even if they're not moving forward in the hiring process. This approach was demonstrated by a fictional letter sent to applicants who didn't get the job, which acknowledged their interest and explained that they were impressed by the candidate's background and skills. However, simply thanking candidates for applying may not be enough. In some cases, employers can go further by providing personalized feedback or even calling candidates directly to inform them of the decision. Companies like Rituals are already taking steps in this direction, offering small gifts as a way of carrying their brand philosophy into recruiting practices. When it comes to candidates who have invested hours in interviews, Salemi recommends that employers take the extra step of reaching out personally to acknowledge their time and effort. The way a company handles its job candidates can reveal a lot about its workplace culture. If employers fail to show appreciation for the time invested by interviewees, potential employees may question how they would be treated as part of the team. Ultimately, treating candidates with dignity and respect is not just about protecting one's reputation, but also doing what's right, according to Salemi. Rejecting candidates in a timely manner, particularly when they reach the final stages of interviews, sends a message that employers value people's time and effort.
